clips.title: Regression Testing for LLMs: Golden Datasets Explained
clips.why: What a golden dataset is and how a regression test runs it, which is what BRAIN-QA is for the brain.
look: The definition of a golden dataset: fixed inputs with expected outputs.
The steps of the regression flow, and where a change gets blocked.
clips.after: BRAIN-QA is our golden dataset; its retrieval step blocks a pull request in rnd-kb that drops below 85%.

clips.title: Regression Testing for LLMs: Golden Datasets Explained
clips.why: How to curate the set: where the cases come from decides whether the test is honest.
look: Listen for where good cases come from: real usage, or invented examples.
Watch whether the set is kept up to date as the product changes, and how.
clips.after: That is why our 60 questions come from what people really asked in public channels, not from the page authors.

clips.title: Agentic Search vs Vector Search for Coding Agents: We Ran the Eval — Braintrust
clips.why: A short case for evals in general: what they are, why "it feels better" is not enough, and which questions they answer.
look: What an eval is, in one sentence.
Why shipping on vibes fails, and what an eval lets a team say instead.
clips.after: A page edit that "reads better" is a vibe; BRAIN-QA's retrieval score is the evidence.

clips.title: Agentic Search vs Vector Search for Coding Agents: We Ran the Eval — Braintrust
clips.why: How the speakers built the dataset for a search eval, a close cousin of BRAIN-QA.
look: Where their questions and expected answers came from.
Ask yourself how a dataset can be kept separate from what is being tested.
clips.after: Our questions live in a restricted repo the brain and the bot cannot read, and a leak check guards the rest.

practice.q: Four of five answerable questions find a source page in the top 5. What is the retrieval score?
practice.why: 4 / 5 = 80%, below the 85% target, so the pull request would fail.

options.text: "Why are my integration tests stuck waiting for the QA lock?", asked in a public channel last month
options.why: A real question in the asker's own words, with a page that answers it.

options.text: "Explain the integration-test-lock runbook", written by the runbook's owner
options.why: It uses the page's own words, so it is always easy to find and tests nothing.

options.text: A question copied from a private channel, word for word
options.why: Private-channel questions are rewritten as summaries, and names are removed.

practice.q: An owner opens a pull request that changes a page. Put what happens in order.
items: kb lint checks the frontmatter, owners, links and paths
The retrieval step runs kb search for every answerable BRAIN-QA question
It counts the questions whose source page is in the top 5
Below 85% the check fails, and the owner sees which case ids missed
That night the answer run asks each question for real, and a judge marks every answer point
practice.why: The cheap, deterministic check guards every change; the expensive judged run follows on a schedule.

practice.q: Someone pastes a question from BRAIN-QA into an FAQ page. What does the leak check do?

options.why: Retrieval passing is exactly the problem: it now passes for the wrong reason.

options.text: It fails, because an 8-word run of the question appears in a page
options.why: The pasted text contains every run of the question, so the check names the case and fails.

practice.q: Why is the judge compared with a person's labels on 10 answers before anyone trusts its numbers?

options.text: Because a judge is a model too, and its marks must agree with a careful person's before they mean anything
options.why: If the judge passes answers a person would fail, the 80% target measures the judge, not the brain.

options.text: Because judges cost too much to run on all 60
options.why: The judge runs on every case every night. The comparison is about trust, not cost.

options.text: Because the person replaces the judge after that
options.why: The person checks the judge once; the judge then runs every night.
